title: The Inheritance of Greywater Bay
premise: When reclusive matriarch Vivienne Ashcroft's will surfaces twelve years after her supposed death, estate lawyer Elodie Marchetti is summoned to Greywater Bay to execute it — only to find the document names her, a stranger, as executor, and the dead woman's death date keeps shifting between copies. When a body washes up wearing clothes stolen from Elodie's own closet, she realizes someone has been living her life from the inside, and the town's meticulously filed secrets are the killer's blueprint. Following a double-entry ledger hidden in the Ashcroft estate's library catalog, Elodie uncovers that Vivienne faked her death to expose a decades-old cover-up — one Elodie's own firm helped bury — and that her missing memories of the summer she left Greywater Bay hold the final key. In the climax she confronts the killer, her estranged half-sister who has been erasing and replacing her identity, and ends the book by choosing to publish the truth, surrendering her career to keep her self.
about_author: Ivo Eastwick is the pen name of a former small-town archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the paper trails of coastal estate disputes. Eastwick writes mysteries where the true crime scene is always the filing cabinet.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A courier delivers a probate petition for Vivienne Ashcroft — dead twelve years, yet dated three weeks ago. Elodie recognizes her own firm's letterhead, forged perfectly, and her own name as executor. The beat is cold dread dressed as professional curiosity; she drives to Greywater Bay against every instinct that told her never to return.

chapters.title: Salt and Statute
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The Ashcroft estate is sealed, dusty, and impossibly lived-in — fresh coffee, a turned-down bed. The town registrar claims no will was ever filed. Elodie finds her childhood nickname written in the guest book, in handwriting she almost recognizes as her own. Emotional beat: the uncanny familiarity of a place she's spent twelve years avoiding.

chapters.title: The Witness in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Police constable Bram Okafor interviews her after she reports the break-in at her rental cottage; nothing stolen, everything rearranged by inches. He mentions a woman matching Elodie's description was seen at the docks last night — while Elodie was asleep. Beat: the first fracture in her certainty about her own alibi.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Alphabetized Silence
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, with flashback. Sorting Vivienne's papers, Elodie recalls the summer she clerked here at nineteen, and the gap in her memory after the night of the Ashcroft boating accident. Her old case notes are missing from the firm's archives — she checked for years. Beat: grief for a version of herself she can't retrieve.

chapters.title: A Body in Borrowed Clothes
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A drowned woman surfaces at Greywater Bay wearing Elodie's missing grey coat and a locket with Elodie's law-school photo inside. The body is identified as Mara Voss, a firm paralegal who vanished in 2013. Beat: Bram's suspicion hardens into something like protectiveness — and Elodie becomes the town's prime suspect.

chapters.title: The Ledger in the Card Catalog
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Following a catalog card misfiled under 'Voss, Mara,' Elodie finds the library's drawers encode a double-entry ledger: debits of money, credits of silence, spanning thirty years of Greywater Bay payments. Her firm's name appears in the margins. Beat: vertigo — the orderly world of her profession revealed as the crime itself.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, harbor master Tull's. Tull recalls the night of the 2013 accident: two girls in one boat, one girl pulled from the water, and a payout that bought his silence about the second. He never saw the second girl's face. Beat: the reader realizes Elodie's missing night is the story's buried heart.

chapters.title: The Executor's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The will's terms surface: she inherits everything only if she 'publishes the ledger within ninety days' — otherwise the estate passes to a trust controlled by her own firm's senior partner, Alistair Crane. Crane arrives in town, all charm, warning her off. Beat: love against duty begins — her duty to the firm versus the truth.

chapters.title: Bram's Cold File
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram reopens the 2013 accident file and finds the investigating officer was paid through the same ledger. He shares it with Elodie off the record, an act of professional self-destruction. Beat: the first true alliance, and the first warmth — two people choosing each other over their institutions.

chapters.title: The Second Set of Keys
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie discovers someone has been entering the estate with a key cut from hers; in the locked study she finds a wall of photographs of herself — her commute, her office, her apartment — taken over years. Beat: terror sharpened into focus. She has been studied the way she studies files.

chapters.title: Mara's Last Filing
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, reading Mara's recovered notebook. Mara had found the ledger first, contacted Vivienne, and helped stage the death to force probate — then got cold feet and tried to sell the ledger back to Crane. Beat: moral complexity; the victim was both whistleblower and blackmailer.

chapters.title: Crane's Offer
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Crane offers Elodie partnership and the firm's protection if she declares the will a forgery and seals the ledger forever. He hints he knows about her missing night — 'accidents happen to girls in boats.' Beat: the seduction of complicity, and Elodie's refusal, quiet and total.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Her
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Searching Vivienne's bedroom, Elodie finds a locked writing desk keyed to a birthdate that isn't Vivienne's — it's Elodie's own. Inside: letters addressed 'To my daughter who doesn't know she's mine.' Beat: identity upended; Elodie is an Ashcroft, and the will was never a stranger's document.

chapters.title: Half of Everything
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, flashback thread. The letters reveal twins separated as children: Elodie raised by the Marchettis, her sister raised by Vivienne and institutionalized after the 2013 accident — the sister who was in the boat, who remembers everything, and who was erased from every record by Crane's firm. Beat: Elodie's amnesia reframed as someone else's wound.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Docks
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Dock camera footage, thought wiped, surfaces on a fish-scaled memory card Tull kept: a woman with Elodie's face watching the cottage the night Mara died — but wearing a scar Elodie doesn't have. Beat: the twin is alive, present, and the killer's identity crystallizes for the reader before Elodie.

chapters.title: Ninety Days to Six
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. With six days left on the will's deadline, Elodie races to authenticate the ledger while someone systematically destroys catalog cards. She reconstructs the destroyed entries from her own professional memory of the firm's files — her twelve years of alphabetizing become the weapon. Beat: her dutiful life repurposed as resistance.

chapters.title: The Confession in the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A note in Elodie's own handwriting lures her to the boathouse at night. Her sister — Calla, alive, gaunt, wearing stolen clothes for years to move through the world as Elodie — confesses to Mara's death, framed as protecting the ledger from a blackmailer, and asks Elodie to remember their accident with her. Beat: pity and horror entwined; the killer is the self Elodie might have been.

chapters.title: What Happened on the Water
chapters.summary: Shared POV, the recovered memory. The 2013 accident: Crane's men pursued the twins' boat to seize evidence of the ledger; the crash wasn't an accident at all. Vivienne saved one daughter and lost the other to the water and to Crane's arrangement — a psychiatric commitment bought with the ledger's silence. Beat: the theme of memory resolved into fact; grief with a target.

chapters.title: Crane's Last Filing
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Crane, exposed by the reconstructed ledger, attempts to burn the estate's library with Elodie inside. Bram and Tull intervene; Crane is arrested on the boathouse dock among his own ash-flecked papers. Beat: climax's first resolution — the institution defeated by the very records it tried to erase.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Bay
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Calla, awaiting trial, asks Elodie not to forgive her but to witness her — to put her name back in the record. Elodie files a petition restoring Calla's identity, her inheritance rights, and her existence in the town's books. Beat: love against duty resolved as a third thing: witness. Not absolution, but acknowledgment.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Will
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, public scene. On the ninety-first day, Elodie publishes the ledger at a town meeting in the Ashcroft library, reading names aloud as the harbor listens — Tull's among them. She resigns from the firm by leaving her partnership letter in the card catalog under 'M.' Beat: catharsis; the town's secrets finally alphabetized in the open.

chapters.title: Greywater, After
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, epilogue. Months later, Elodie stays on as the estate's archivist, cataloguing the Ashcroft papers with Calla's letters filed beside Vivienne's. Bram brings coffee; the bay does what bays do. Final beat: memory as inheritance — she keeps the records now, but this time they belong to everyone.
